paper_a.title: A new proof of a Liouville theorem for the one dimensional Gross-Pitaevskii equation

paper_b.title: A New proof of Liouville type theorems for a class of semilinear elliptic equations

metadata.description: Both papers re-prove Liouville-type rigidity theorems for nonlinear PDE by following the same high-level template: construct an algebraic differential identity from the equation, integrate it (in time for the dispersive GP equation in paper A, in space against a cut-off for the elliptic equation in paper B), and use a coercive functional plus a controlled remainder to force the solution to be trivial / a single soliton. The mathematical settings (dispersive 1D Gross-Pitaevskii vs stationary semilinear elliptic on R^n / closed manifold) and the concrete algebraic devices (Darboux-style operator factorization L+ = Sc* Sc plus virial identity vs Ma-Wu invariant tensor E_ij plus Bochner-type identity) are different, so most node-level matches are analogous rather than exact, but the proof skeletons line up step-for-step which justifies the SM tag from the master CSV.

matches.explanation: Both are the master nonlinear PDE under study. Paper A's 1D Gross-Pitaevskii equation $i\partial_t\psi+\partial_x^2\psi+\psi(1-|\psi|^2)=0$ is a time-dependent dispersive equation with non-vanishing boundary conditions, while paper B's $\Delta u + f(u)=0$ (with the model case $\Delta u + u^p = 0$) is a stationary semilinear elliptic equation. Same role (the equation whose solutions the Liouville theorem rigidifies), fundamentally different PDE class.

Paper A's explicit dark/black soliton family $U_c$ has no counterpart in paper B; semilinear elliptic Liouville theorems on R^n with subcritical $f$ rigidify to the trivial / constant solution rather than to a non-trivial profile family. The notion of a moving soliton is intrinsic to the dispersive setting.

The Hamiltonian / energy functional $E(\psi)$ for GP is a conserved Hamiltonian specific to the dispersive setting; paper B does not introduce a conserved energy because its equation is stationary and the integration happens in space against cut-offs.

The energy space $\mathcal{E}$ for GP solutions (continuous functions with $\psi'\in L^2$ and $1-|\psi|^2\in L^2$) is dictated by the non-vanishing-at-infinity boundary condition; paper B works with smooth positive solutions on R^n or a closed manifold and has no analogous functional space.

The exponentially weighted norms with $\rho=\sech$ are tailored to the spatial decay of the linearized operators around solitons. Paper B uses smooth compactly supported cut-offs $\eta$ instead of intrinsic exponential weights; no direct counterpart.
The metric $d$ on the energy space $\mathcal{E}$ is specific to GP. Paper B has no analogous distance because it works pointwise / via integral inequalities on positive scalar functions.

Both nodes introduce the algebraic objects on which the entire identity machinery is built: paper A's first-order operators $S_c, S_c^\star$ together with the linearized operators $L_\pm$ around the soliton density $Q_c$, and paper B's invariant trace-free tensor $E_{ij}$ defined from $\nabla u$. They play the same role as the bespoke algebraic constructions tailored to the equation, but the construction (operator factorization vs conformal-type tensor) is different. Both are flagged as `external` in their respective papers' citations (Bethuel-Gravejat-Smets / Gravejat-Smets vs Ma-Wu).

The control functional $\mathcal{N}$ packages $w_1, \partial_x w_2, \partial_x^2 w_2$ in $L^2$; paper B uses pointwise integrals of $|\nabla u|^4$ and $f^2(u)$ against cut-offs and weights instead of a single packaged norm, so there is no direct counterpart.

The bounded virial functional $\mathcal{I}=\int x(\partial_x w_2)(w_1-c\partial_x w_2)$ is specific to a time-dependent virial argument: $\dot{\mathcal{I}}$ is forced positive while $\mathcal{I}$ stays bounded in time, hence integration in time produces a finite integral of the coercive functional. Paper B has no time variable; the analogue is integration of the algebraic identity in space against $\eta^\gamma$, and the corresponding `bounded primitive' trick is not used.

The Darboux-type factorization identity $L_+=S_c^\star S_c$ and $S_c(L_- - c^2)S_c^\star=(\partial_x^2-\beta^2)\partial_x^2$ is the key spectral lemma that converts the linearized GP problem into a potential-free transformed problem in $(w_1, w_2)$. Paper B has no spectral / operator factorization; its algebraic device is a pointwise tensor identity instead.
Inversion of the operator $S_c^\star$ with explicit kernel and weighted estimates; entirely tied to the operator factorization machinery, no counterpart in paper B.

Coercivity bounds that recover $\epsilon_1, \epsilon_2$ (the modulation remainder) from the transformed variables $w_1, w_2$ and from the functional $\mathcal{N}$. These are bookkeeping lemmas internal to the GP factorization-virial pipeline; paper B has no modulation remainder so no analogue.

Estimates on parameter time-derivatives $\dot a, \dot c, \dot\theta$ and forcing terms $F_1, F_2$ are specific to the modulation framework used for the time-dependent GP problem. Paper B has no time-dependent modulation.

Weighted Sobolev / Cauchy-Schwarz tools for the energy space $\mathcal{E}$; analogue technical lemmas in paper B (Cauchy-Schwarz / Young / Holder used inside PP467.3 and PP467.4) are inlined into the proofs rather than packaged as a named lemma.
The transformed system in $(w_1, w_2)$ is the central output of the operator-factorization step that paper B does not have.

Core algebraic identity of each paper. Paper A's virial identity $\dot{\mathcal{I}}=\frac12\mathcal{Q}+\mathcal{R}$ writes a time derivative of the bounded functional $\mathcal{I}$ as a coercive quadratic form $\mathcal{Q}$ plus a remainder $\mathcal{R}$. Paper B's key invariant-tensor identity writes a divergence $u^{2\beta/(n+2)}(u^{-2\beta/(n+2)}E_{ij}u^j)^i$ as $|E_{ij}|^2$ + a curvature-style $|\nabla u|^4 / u^2$ coefficient + Ricci term + a subcritical $(f' - \beta f/u)|\nabla u|^2$ term. Both are pointwise/derivative identities that, after integration (in time vs in space), produce coercive control on a positive integrand modulo a sign-controlled remainder. Same structural role; different algebraic content.

The coercivity lemma $\mathcal{Q}\geq\frac{\beta^2}{16}\mathcal{N}^2$ states that the quadratic form coming out of the virial identity dominates the $\mathcal{N}^2$ functional. Paper B's analogous coercivity is built into the key identity itself (the $|E_{ij}|^2$ term plus the $|\nabla u|^4$ term with explicitly positive coefficient $\beta(1-(n-2)\beta/(n+2))$), rather than being stated as a separate lemma. Listed as `none` because there is no L1 parent on the B side that isolates the coercivity claim.

Both nodes provide the auxiliary integral / pointwise estimates needed to control the error term in the main rigidity identity. Paper A's $|\mathcal{R}|\lesssim\mathcal{N}^3$ bounds the cubic remainder of the virial identity by the coercive quantity to power 3/2 of itself, allowing an absorption argument. Paper B's two integral inequalities (LP467.1 bounding $\int u^{-2\beta/(n+2)-2}|\nabla u|^4 \eta^\gamma$ and LP467.2 bounding $\int u^{-2\beta/(n+2)} f^2\eta^\gamma$) play the analogous role, controlling the would-be error / coercivity-loss terms by a cut-off integral that vanishes as $R\to\infty$. Different objects, parallel role.

Both sides give the punch-line proof that bundles the pointwise identity, the coercivity, and the remainder estimate to force triviality. Paper A's PP466.1 combines Lemmas 7, 8, 9 to get $\dot{\mathcal{I}}\gtrsim\mathcal{N}^2$, integrates in time using $\mathcal{I}$ bounded, deduces $\int_\mathbb{R}\mathcal{N}^2<\infty$, picks $t_n\to\infty$ with $\mathcal{N}(t_n)\to0$, and uses orbital stability to conclude $\psi$ is exactly a soliton. Paper B's three Liouville proofs (PP467.2 closed-manifold, PP467.4 Euclidean super-power, PP467.5 dimension-split) integrate the key identity over $M$ or against a cut-off in $\mathbb{R}^n$, use sign analysis / Holder / Young to get integral estimates whose right-hand side vanishes as the domain or cut-off scale grows, and conclude triviality. Same template (algebraic identity $\rightarrow$ integrate $\rightarrow$ vanishing argument), realised in the time vs space direction.
Proof of the operator factorization lemma; intrinsic to paper A's spectral approach.
Proof of the inversion-of-$S_c^\star$ lemma; intrinsic to paper A's factorization toolkit.
Proofs of the coercivity bounds for $\epsilon_1, \epsilon_2$ via the transformed variables; bookkeeping inside the modulation/factorization framework with no counterpart in paper B.
Proof of the parameter-derivative / forcing-term estimates. Modulation-specific.

Both are the `derivation of the central pointwise identity' proof. Paper A's PP466.7 differentiates $\mathcal{I}$ in time, substitutes the transformed-system equations for $\partial_t w_1, \partial_t w_2$, and integrates by parts to obtain $\dot{\mathcal{I}}=\frac12\mathcal{Q}+\mathcal{R}$. Paper B's PP467.1 computes $E_{ij}^i$ via the Ricci identity, substitutes $(\Delta u)_j=-f'(u)u_j$, contracts with $u^j$, and absorbs a residual via a conformal weight to obtain the key identity. Same proof template (differentiate the candidate object, substitute the equation, regroup to a quadratic-plus-remainder form).

Proof of the coercivity $\mathcal{Q}\geq\frac{\beta^2}{16}\mathcal{N}^2$; algebraic regrouping internal to paper A. Paper B's coercivity is absorbed into the key identity itself rather than proved separately.

Both proofs establish the auxiliary error / integral bounds needed in the main proof. Paper A's PP466.9 splits $\mathcal{R}=\mathcal{R}_1+\mathcal{R}_2+\mathcal{R}_3$ and bounds each by Cauchy-Schwarz against the weighted estimates of Lemmas 4-6 to get $|\mathcal{R}|\lesssim\mathcal{N}^3$. Paper B's PP467.3 multiplies the key identity by $\eta^\gamma$, integrates by parts the divergence term, and applies Cauchy-Schwarz / Young / subcriticality to derive Lemmas LP467.1 and LP467.2. Same `Cauchy-Schwarz against the weighted/cut-off estimates' style.
Proof of the weighted Sobolev tools lemma. Analogous Holder / Young manipulations in paper B are not packaged as a separate proof.

Paper B's Main Theorem 1 (closed manifold case) has no counterpart in paper A. Paper A is set on the line $\mathbb{R}$ for a time-dependent equation with no manifold geometry; rigidity on closed manifolds with $\mathrm{Ric}\ge 0$ is intrinsic to the elliptic Bochner-style approach.

Main Theorem 2 (Euclidean Liouville under subcritical + super-power lower bound on $f$) is the elliptic Liouville statement itself; paper A's analogous statement is the cited TP466.1 (external Bethuel-Gravejat-Smets / Gravejat-Smets theorem), so this paper-original B theorem matches no paper-original A node.

Main Theorem 3 (Euclidean dimension-split: $n=3$ with $u$ bounded vs $n\geq 4$ with super-power $f$) is a paper-B-original statement on $\mathbb{R}^n$ with no counterpart in the 1D dispersive setting of paper A.

The subcritical condition $\beta f(u) - u f'(u) \ge 0$ on the nonlinearity $f$ is intrinsic to the semilinear-elliptic Liouville framework. Paper A's nonlinearity is the fixed cubic $\psi(1-|\psi|^2)$, with no analogous family-level subcriticality hypothesis.
Definition of the squared norm of a second-order tensor on a Riemannian manifold; intrinsic to paper B's tensor calculus and has no analogue in paper A.
